passage:
Sunday night, hostel.
What a match. When the last ball went for four, the whole East Stand jumped at once. Strangers hugged me. Pranav lifted me off my feet, screaming. I've never felt joy like that in a crowd, like one big body.
Then it changed, fast. At the exit ramp people kept surging forward, still singing, but the singing turned into shoving. My arms got pinned. A man behind us yelled "Push!" and nobody could. I saw Pranav's face go pale. Remembering the side gate we had noticed on the way in, I grabbed his sleeve and we edged sideways along the wall till we got out.
We stood on the road shaking and laughing at the same time. Next match: we pick the exit before the first ball, and we leave five minutes early if the ramp looks packed.
— Mridul

qa.q: Which gate did Mridul and Pranav use to get out?
qa.a: The side gate they had noticed on the way in.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when the whole stand jumped at the last ball?
qa.a: Mridul felt pure joy, like the crowd was one big body; later that joy turned into fear when the shoving started at the exit.

qa.q: Which choice kept Mridul and Pranav safe, and what is their plan now?
qa.a: Edging sideways along the wall to the side gate got them out; next time they will pick the exit early and leave before the ramp packs.

qa.q: What was it like for Pranav when the crowd began shoving?
qa.a: His face went pale, suggesting he was frightened once the singing crowd became a crush.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading crowd hugging and jumping as shared joy, then noticing the shift to unsafe pushing and using an exit plan.

passage: The kabaddi final at the Mandvi village fair ended with the home team winning by one point. The crowd poured onto the dusty ground, dancing to the dhol, lifting the players up. Pooja and Sonali danced too, arms in the air. Then Pooja noticed the rope around the ground sagging as more people pressed in from the road side. A small boy near the rope was crying, squeezed between two men. The drumming went on, but the shouts now sounded different, sharper. "Sonali, we're going to the temple steps," Pooja said, taking her friend's hand. On the way she lifted the crying boy up to a man from his village, who carried him out. From the temple steps, higher up, they watched the crowd thin slowly. Sonali was still grinning. "You spoil every party," she teased. Pooja just pointed at the fallen rope.

qa.a: The crowd poured onto the dusty ground, dancing to the dhol and lifting the players up.

A shove sent one of the men staggering towards them. Irfan dropped low, arm over his head, and pulled Lalit down beside him behind a bench. Then they stood and walked quickly to the tea shop at the end of the stand. Irfan told the shopkeeper, who knew the station guard, and the guard came with his whistle. The crowd parted. Lalit muttered that he could have handled it. "Maybe," Irfan said. "But I want to be on that bus, not in the hospital."

passage: Friday night in a crowded bar in Gothenburg, Astrid and Yara were celebrating Yara's new job when voices rose at the next table. A glass shattered on the floor. Astrid's body moved before she thought: she dropped into a crouch, hands over her head, and tugged Yara down with her. For a second she felt ridiculous. Then another glass flew past the space where Yara's head had been. The bouncer was already pushing through. Astrid stood slowly. "We're leaving," she said. Yara hesitated; her coat was on the chair near the fight. "Leave it. We'll come back tomorrow." Outside in the cold, Astrid told a second staff member at the door what had happened and which table it was. Yara hugged her, shivering. "I thought you were overreacting." Astrid laughed shakily. "So did I, for about one second."

passage: Listen, Wasim, you asked why I always ask new trainees how they're doing, so I'll tell you. I'm Pranav uncle to you all now, but at twenty I worked the night shift at a print press with my friend Gopal. Our supervisor had a loud voice and a heavy hand on the desk. I noticed Gopal would flinch every time the man came near, step back half a pace, cross his arms tight over his chest. At first I told myself Gopal was just tired. Then one night I saw him wince when the supervisor clapped his shoulder. I didn't say anything in front of anyone. At the tea break, outside, I just asked, "Gopal, is everything okay with him?" Gopal said nothing for a long time. Then he talked. I listened, and I told him about the workers' welfare officer. He went the next week. It was his choice. I only walked with him to the door.

qa.q: Where did young Pranav and Gopal work?
qa.a: On the night shift at a print press.

qa.q: What might Gopal have been feeling when the supervisor came near?

passage: Lunch at the call centre was exactly twenty minutes, and the queue for the microwave took ten. Seema had noticed it all week: whenever team leader Harsh walked past, Nitin went very still, pulled his chair in and hunched over his keyboard. Once, when Harsh leaned over his shoulder, Nitin jerked his head back as if expecting a blow. It could be nothing. Maybe Nitin just hated being watched. But Seema couldn't shake it. With eight minutes left, she found Nitin on the back stairs with his tiffin. "Can I sit?" He nodded. "I've seen you tense up when Harsh comes by. You don't have to tell me anything. I just wanted to ask if you're okay." Nitin stared at his rice. "He shouts at me when nobody's around." Seema listened, then said, "HR has a confidential complaints line. I can sit with you when you call, or not. Your call." The bell rang. Nitin said, "Stay after shift?" She stayed.

Was he embarrassed because his module was behind? Or just shocked? She couldn't tell. After the meeting, at the water cooler, she asked, "You okay? You looked stunned in there." Asif laughed a little. "Stunned is right. I was about to say, 'Are you serious?' out loud. The hand stopped me." Ishita laughed. "I thought you were ashamed of your module." "That too, maybe," he admitted. "A bit of both."

passage:
Supervisor's note, internship programme, week four.
A colleague mentioned that our intern Joseph was "restless and rude" in meetings: clicking his pen, bouncing his leg under the table. I watched on Wednesday. The clicking did not stop while he listened, but his notes were the most complete in the room, and he asked the only question about the delivery dates. I spoke to Joseph privately afterwards and asked, with no complaint in my voice, whether the pen helped him. He looked worried at first, then said he is neurodivergent and that moving helps him concentrate; when he sits still, he loses the thread. I thanked him for telling me. I offered him a silent clicker so the noise would not bother anyone, and he chose that himself. I have told the team that movement is not inattention, and I will check with Joseph in a fortnight.
— Elizabeth

qa.q: What did Joseph ask about in the Wednesday meeting?
qa.a: The delivery dates.

qa.q: How did Joseph seem to feel when Elizabeth first asked about the pen?
qa.a: He looked worried, perhaps expecting a complaint, and then seemed more at ease once he could explain that moving helps him concentrate.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth do that respected Joseph's way of focusing?
qa.a: She watched before judging, asked privately without blame, let Joseph choose a silent clicker, and told the team movement is not inattention.

qa.q: How did the colleague read Joseph's pen clicking and leg bouncing?
qa.a: The colleague read it as restless and rude, not knowing it was how Joseph stayed focused.

grounding: Shows a young adult using pen clicking and leg bouncing to focus, and a supervisor helping others not read it as rudeness.

passage:
12 March, library, 6 p.m.
Today I got the reading on transport policy finally, all of it, the whole argument clicked, and my hands started flapping before I could stop them. Happy flapping. It's how my body says yes. Then I saw the boy at the next table staring and I sat on my hands. Old habit. I felt my chest go tight.
Ten minutes later Yusuf from my tutorial came by and said, quite gently, "I saw you flapping. Are you okay, or was that a good thing?" Nobody has ever asked me that. I said it was a very good thing. He said his little cousin does it when she's excited, and he just wanted to check. Then he went back to his desk like it was normal. It is normal, for me. I took my hands out from under my legs and kept reading.
— Vandana

qa.a: The reading on transport policy.

qa.a: Vandana felt self-conscious, chest tightening, and sat on both hands; the flapping itself had come from happiness at understanding the reading.

qa.a: It felt new and freeing; being asked let Vandana take both hands out and keep reading without hiding.

passage: Looking back at that week after Shalini's breakup, I think I learnt more about my little sister than in all our years sharing a room. passage:
Ward nurse's note, women's surgical ward, night shift.
Bed 12, Zainab, 22, day one after her operation. Her husband, Yogesh, sat with her all evening. I noticed he kept stroking the back of her hand very lightly, and each time she settled and her breathing slowed. Around eleven her pain rose. When he reached for her hand, she pulled it away and turned her face. He froze, then took his hand back and asked quietly, "Do you want me to stop, or just be here?" She said, "Just be here." He sat back with his hands in his lap. I gave her the medicine the doctor had charted and checked her after half an hour. By midnight she held her hand out to him herself, and he took it. I reminded him visiting would end soon; he said goodnight softly. Will pass on at handover that the family is a good support.

qa.a: He kept stroking the back of her hand very lightly.

qa.a: It shows touch comforts only when welcome: Yogesh stopped at once when Zainab pulled away, asked, and waited until she offered her hand again.

passage:
Thursday, late.
Manoj came over after the call from his dad. He sat on my sofa with his head in his hands and didn't say much. I sat next to him and, without thinking, started stroking his hair, the way he likes on lazy Sundays. He leaned into it for a minute. Then he went tense and moved his head away. I stopped straight away and asked, "Not now?" He said, "Sorry. I just feel like I'll fall apart if you're too soft right now." I told him nothing to be sorry for. I made tea instead and sat with my knee touching his, which he seemed fine with. Later, when he got up to leave, he hugged me for a long time, and said thanks for listening. I keep thinking: the same touch that helps on Sunday can be too much on a Thursday like this.
— Nazia

qa.q: What had happened before Manoj came over?
qa.a: The call from his dad.

qa.a: He was upset and afraid he would fall apart if things felt too soft; he seemed embarrassed too, since he apologised.

qa.a: Nazia stopped straight away, asked "Not now?", and switched to tea and a small knee touch Manoj seemed fine with.

passage: The 6:40 local was so packed that Irawati could barely lift her arm to hold the rail. At Dadar more people pushed in, and a man behind her pressed closer than the crowd needed. His hand brushed her waist, then stayed. Irawati's whole body went cold. There was nowhere to step. She turned her head and said, loud and firm, "Move your hand. Now." He didn't. She shoved his wrist away hard with her elbow. Her friend Keerthana, two people away, saw her face and forced her way over. "Stand with me," Keerthana said, pulling Irawati against the door, her own body between them. At the next station they got down, and Keerthana waved over the railway police constable on the platform. Irawati described the man's shirt and the coach number. The constable radioed ahead. Irawati's hands were shaking, but she felt proud she had said it out loud.

passage: At the office party in Gurugram, Nilesh from accounts kept draping his arm over Rehana's shoulder while telling stories, laughing loudly. The first time she slid out from under it. The second time she stepped back. The third time, she turned to face him, raised one palm between them and said clearly, "Please don't put your arm on me." The group went quiet. Nilesh's face went red. He lifted his arm away at once. "Oh. Sorry, sorry. I didn't realise." He took a step back and put his hands in his pockets. Rehana's heart was hammering, but she nodded. "Thanks." Later he came up to her near the snacks and said, "I'm used to my friends from college. I should have asked. It won't happen again." Rehana said, "Okay," and meant it, though she stayed at the other end of the room for the rest of the evening.

qa.q: What did Rehana raise between them when she spoke?
qa.a: One palm.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when she spoke up the third time?
qa.a: She was nervous, her heart hammering, but determined; afterwards she seemed relieved and still a little wary, staying at the other end of the room.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do right once Rehana set the boundary?
qa.a: He stopped at once, stepped back, apologised without arguing, and later took responsibility instead of making excuses.

qa.q: How might the people in the group have seen the moment?
qa.a: They went quiet, likely surprised; seeing Nilesh stop at once may have shown them that a clear no should be respected immediately.

grounding: Shows a young adult using a raised palm, a step away and a firm request to set a boundary, and the other person stopping at once.

passage:
"Your left elbow is dropping," Jagdish said, reaching for Mahima's arm.
"You can just tell me," Mahima said, stepping back. "I'd rather you didn't touch me to correct it."
"It's faster this way. All trainers do it."
"I know. I'm still asking you not to."
He laughed. "Relax, madam." His hand went to her lower back to push her posture.
Mahima twisted away and pushed his hand off. "No. I said no."
"Okay, okay, so sensitive."
Mahima put the dumbbells down. She picked up her bag and walked to the front desk.
"I want to speak to the manager," she told the receptionist, voice shaking a little. "The trainer touched me after I asked him not to."
The manager came out within a minute. "Thank you for telling me. I'm taking him off your sessions from today, and I'll note it formally. Would you like a different trainer?"
"Yes," Mahima said. "One who listens."

qa.q: Where did Mahima go after putting the dumbbells down?
qa.a: She walked to the front desk.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when she went to the front desk?
qa.a: She was upset and shaken, her voice shaking a little, but determined to report it after her no was ignored.

qa.q: Which choice worked when Jagdish ignored Mahima's request?
qa.a: Pushing his hand off, leaving the session and reporting to the manager worked, since the manager removed him and noted it formally.

qa.q: How did the gym manager respond, and why does that matter?
qa.a: The manager thanked Mahima, took Jagdish off her sessions that day and noted it, showing her report was taken seriously.

grounding: Shows a young adult setting a touch boundary, pushing away when it is ignored, and leaving and reporting it.

subtype: Touch norms across cultures and settings [Mismatch]
passage: On his first week at a Bengaluru design studio, Vikas did what he'd always done at his last job in Delhi: a friendly slap on the shoulder when a colleague made a good point. When he did it to Santosh, a quiet senior from Kerala, Santosh flinched and edged his chair away. Vikas felt his stomach twist. Had he offended him? At lunch he noticed the others. Priyanka high-fived only her close friends. Santosh greeted everyone with a small nod and no touch at all. Later, while walking to the lift, Vikas asked, "Santosh, earlier, the shoulder thing, was that too much?" Santosh smiled, a little relieved. "A bit. I'm not much of a touching person at work. A nod is fine." Vikas nodded. The next time Santosh fixed his layout, Vikas gave him a thumbs-up across the desk instead.

qa.q: Where had Vikas worked before?
qa.a: At his last job in Delhi.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when Santosh flinched?
qa.a: He felt worried and a bit guilty, his stomach twisting, wondering whether he had offended Santosh.

qa.q: What small step helped Vikas understand Santosh?
qa.a: He watched how others greeted each other and then asked Santosh privately whether the shoulder slap had been too much.

qa.q: How did Santosh experience the shoulder slap?
qa.a: It felt like too much at work, which is why he flinched and moved his chair; he seemed relieved when Vikas asked.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning that a shoulder slap friendly in one workplace can feel intrusive in another, and asking how a colleague prefers to be greeted.

subtype: Touch norms across cultures and settings [Mismatch]
passage:
"So when we get to your house, I hug your dad, right?" Samir asked, adjusting his collar in the auto.
Jomon laughed. "Appachan? No. He'll shake your hand. Firmly. Maybe a pat on your arm if he likes you."
"My dad would be offended if you didn't hug him."
"I know! Remember last Eid? He nearly lifted me off the ground." Jomon grinned. "Here it's different. Ammachi won't shake hands at all. Just smile and say hello."
"And your grandmother? Do I touch her feet?"
"She'd be surprised. We don't really do that. A namaskaram with folded hands is lovely though."
Samir groaned. "How do you remember all this?"
"I don't. I watch. And if I'm not sure, I just ask. You can ask Appachan too. He likes being asked."
The auto stopped at the gate. Appachan was already on the verandah, hand out. Samir shook it.

qa.q: How does Jomon say Appachan will greet Samir?
qa.a: He'll shake your hand. Firmly.

qa.q: How was Samir feeling on the way to Jomon's house?
qa.a: He was nervous about getting the greeting wrong, fussing with his collar and asking about each person; he may also have felt a little overwhelmed by the differences.

qa.q: What advice does Jomon give that Samir could use in any new home?
qa.a: Watch how people greet each other, and if unsure, simply ask how they prefer to be greeted.

qa.q: How would Samir's dad feel if Jomon greeted him the way Appachan prefers?
qa.a: He would feel offended by just a handshake, since in his home a hug shows warmth.

grounding: Shows two young adults comparing how hugs, handshakes, feet-touching and folded hands carry different meanings in different families, and choosing to watch and ask.

subtype: Touch norms across cultures and settings [Mismatch]
passage: I still wince remembering my first week in Lyon. I'm Bidisha, and I'd grown up touching my elders' feet and hugging my friends tight. At a dinner at my classmate Avni's host family, the grandmother leaned in to kiss my cheeks. I panicked and bent down to touch her feet instead. She stumbled back, confused, and everyone laughed, kindly but loudly. My face burned. Avni, who'd been there three months already, pulled me aside later. "Here it's two kisses on the cheek, but only when they offer. Watch first." Over the next weeks I did. The bakery lady never touched anyone. Colleagues at my internship just shook hands. Close friends did the cheek kisses. I learnt to wait half a second and let the other person lead. By the end, I could greet Avni's host grandmother properly. She patted my cheek and said I was learning well.

qa.q: What did the grandmother lean in to do?
qa.a: To kiss Bidisha's cheeks.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when everyone laughed?
qa.a: Bidisha felt embarrassed, face burning, even though the laughter was kind; the panic just before shows Bidisha was anxious about the unfamiliar greeting.

qa.q: What habit helped Bidisha avoid more awkward greetings?
qa.a: Waiting half a second and letting the other person lead, after watching how people greeted in different settings.

qa.q: What was it like for the grandmother when Bidisha bent to touch her feet?
qa.a: She stumbled back, confused, because a gesture of respect in Bidisha's culture was unfamiliar and surprising to her.

grounding: Shows a young adult finding that cheek kisses, handshakes and touching elders' feet carry different meanings in different settings, and learning to watch and follow.

passage:
Hi Joseph,
You asked what's been strangest about moving to Helsinki. It isn't the cold. It's the space between people.
My first morning I stood at a bus stop about a foot behind a woman, like at home in Pune. She moved away. I stepped closer to stay in the queue, and she moved again. I thought she found me rude or even scary. Then I noticed everyone else: two metres apart, each person in their own bubble, and nobody offended by it.
In the office it's the same. When I lean in to talk, my colleague Aino leans back. At first I read it as coldness. Now I think it's just normal distance here, and she's actually quite warm once you know her. I've started standing further back. It still feels unfriendly to me, honestly. But I think it's only different.
Write soon,
Yogesh

qa.q: How far apart did Yogesh notice people standing at the bus stop?
qa.a: Two metres apart.

qa.q: What did Yogesh first think when the woman at the bus stop moved away?
qa.a: Yogesh felt unsure and a bit hurt, thinking she found Yogesh rude or even scary; it later seemed she was just keeping normal local distance.

qa.q: What change has Yogesh made, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Standing further back, which matches local spacing and stops others from reading Yogesh's closeness as pushy.

qa.q: How might Aino see Yogesh's leaning in to talk?
qa.a: She may find it a bit too close for comfort, which is why she leans back, even though she is warm once people know her.

grounding: Shows a young adult abroad finding that conversation distance and queue spacing differ, and learning to read stepping back as difference rather than coldness.

passage: So, Pooja, you want the Rio story? Okay. I'm Baljeet, right, and I thought I was a pretty close talker, being a Punjabi girl. Then I went to Brazil for my exchange semester. On my first day, a classmate named Lucas came up to introduce himself and stood so close I could smell his coffee. I stepped back. He stepped forward. I stepped back again, right into a plant pot! He must have thought I didn't like him. And I thought he was being pushy. Later my flatmate Carla laughed and told me that's just how close people talk there, and that stepping back so much can seem cold. The next week I tried to hold my ground. It felt strange, but the conversations got warmer. And Lucas? He's still my closest friend from that trip.

qa.q: What did Baljeet step back into on the first day?
qa.a: A plant pot.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when Lucas stood so close?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and read him as pushy, which is why she kept stepping back; she later realised he was just being friendly by local habits.

qa.q: What choice turned things around with Lucas?
qa.a: After Carla explained, Baljeet chose to hold her ground instead of stepping back, and the conversations got warmer.

qa.q: What might Lucas have thought when Baljeet kept stepping back?
qa.a: He may have thought she didn't like him or was cold, since close talk was normal for him.

grounding: Shows a young adult abroad learning that conversation distance varies, so stepping back can look cold and stepping in can look pushy, and adjusting gently.

passage: I'm Rekha. I'd been in Tokyo three weeks when my classmate Asif arrived from Hyderabad, and I watched him learn the spaces the hard way. At the train platform he walked straight to the front of the neat line painted on the floor, not realising it was a queue. A businessman stared. Asif went pink and moved to the back. On the train he took the empty seat right next to an elderly woman, though the whole bench was free. She gathered her bag closer and looked away. Maybe she was just tidying, maybe not. At the ramen shop, though, he sat elbow to elbow with strangers at the counter, because that's how everyone sat, and nobody minded. By the second week I noticed him pausing at every door, watching first, then choosing where to stand. He never said much about it, but he stopped looking so tense.

qa.q: Where did Asif sit on the train?
qa.a: In the empty seat right next to an elderly woman.

qa.q: What might Asif have been feeling when the businessman stared?
qa.a: He went pink, so he likely felt embarrassed on realising he had jumped the queue; Rekha can only guess from his face.

qa.q: What habit did Asif build that helped him?
qa.a: Pausing at every door to watch first, then choosing where to stand, which let him match local spacing.

qa.q: How might the elderly woman on the train have felt when Asif sat right beside her?
qa.a: She may have felt crowded since the bench was empty, though Rekha admits her gathering the bag could just have been tidying.

grounding: Shows a young adult abroad, seen by an observer, learning that queue spacing and seating norms differ and adjusting by watching.

subtype: Turning toward and away in conversation [Interpreting]
passage: The evening bus to Sultanpur was late again. Kishore stood at the kasba bus stand telling his friend Ramesh about the new tractor workshop he wanted to start. As he spoke, Ramesh's body turned slowly away, his shoulders and feet pointing towards the road, though his head still nodded. Kishore faltered. Was Ramesh bored? Was the idea stupid? He stopped mid-sentence. "You're not listening, are you?" Ramesh turned back fully, surprised. "I am! I'm watching for the bus. If it comes and I miss it, Amma will kill me. Tell me the rest, about the welding." Kishore laughed, relieved, and kept talking. Ramesh stayed half-turned, one eye on the road, asking about the rent and the tools. When the bus finally came, he said, "Come home Sunday. Tell me properly then."

qa.q: What did Kishore want to start?
qa.a: A new tractor workshop.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when Ramesh turned towards the road?
qa.a: He felt unsure and a bit hurt, wondering if Ramesh was bored or the idea was stupid; once he asked, he felt relieved.

qa.q: What worked better for Kishore than guessing?
qa.a: Asking Ramesh directly, which showed the turn was about watching for the bus, not lack of interest.

qa.q: How did Ramesh see his own turning away?
qa.a: To Ramesh it was just keeping an eye on the road so he wouldn't miss the bus; he was still interested and even invited Kishore to talk more on Sunday.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading a listener's body turning away as disinterest, and learning by asking that it was a need to watch for the bus.

subtype: Turning toward and away in conversation [Interpreting]
passage: In a busy café in Istanbul, Yosef was telling Elif about the internship he'd been offered in Ankara. At first she sat square to him, knees pointing his way, nodding. Halfway through, she shifted in her chair, her body turning toward the door, her bag pulled onto her lap. Yosef slowed down. Was she upset he might move? He didn't want to guess. "Elif, you've turned toward the door. Should I stop?" Elif looked startled, then sheepish. "Sorry, my sister's supposed to pick me up at four and she hates waiting. I didn't mean to look like I was leaving you." She turned her chair back a little. "But I also feel strange about you going to Ankara. That's true too." Yosef nodded. "Can we finish this tomorrow, properly?" Elif smiled. "Yes. Same table."

qa.q: Where was Yosef's internship?
qa.a: In Ankara.

qa.q: What was Elif feeling when she turned toward the door?
qa.a: She was mainly anxious about keeping her sister waiting, but she also admits she feels strange about Yosef moving, so the turn carried more than one feeling.

qa.q: What small step did Yosef take instead of guessing?
qa.a: He named what he saw and asked if he should stop, which let Elif explain both reasons.

qa.q: What would change if Yosef had assumed Elif was uninterested?
qa.a: He might have felt hurt and cut the talk short, never hearing that she had to leave and also felt strange about him going.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing a listener turning away, treating it as a soft cue, and asking rather than guessing.

subtype: Turning toward and away in conversation [Interpreting]
passage: At the weekly one-to-one in the Pune office, Chaitanya pitched his idea for a faster testing checklist. Damini, his manager, started by turning her chair fully toward him, notebook open. Five minutes in, she swivelled halfway back to her laptop, eyes flicking to the screen. Chaitanya's voice went thin. Was she brushing him off? He took a breath. "Damini, I can see something's pulling at you. Should I come back later?" She turned toward him again and let out a breath. "Sorry. The client's escalation email is due any minute, and I promised to reply at once. Your idea is good. Can you send me the checklist and book fifteen minutes tomorrow at ten?" Chaitanya nodded. On his way out, he noticed she had already starred his name in her notes.

qa.q: When did Damini ask Chaitanya to book fifteen minutes?
qa.a: Tomorrow at ten.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya worried about when Damini swivelled back to her laptop?
qa.a: He was anxious that she was brushing off his idea, his voice going thin; it turned out she was waiting for an urgent client email.

qa.a: He named it gently and offered to come back, instead of assuming disinterest or pushing on.

qa.a: She was torn between the pitch and an urgent client email; she thought the idea was good and wanted to give it proper time.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing a listener turning away, treating it as a soft cue, and asking rather than guessing.
